comments.note: CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals requires equal-length byte arrays to guarantee constant time. Both hashes are always produced by Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher (64 hex chars), so equal length is guaranteed by the hasher contract. If stored hash is ever persisted from an external source with a different length, FixedTimeEquals would short-circuit early. Low risk for current design; worth noting for the security auditor.
No test for empty string input to VerifyAsync or SetAsync. Implementation handles it correctly (hashes empty string), but the path is untested.

summary: Reviewed PasswordService.cs, Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs, and test file. 0 Critical, 0 High. 1 Medium: SHA-256+fixed salt is a weak KDF (documented and accepted for local desktop threat model; IPasswordHasher upgrade path available). 1 Low: IPasswordHasher.Verify exposes non-constant-time comparison API (bypassed correctly by PasswordService). CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals usage confirmed correct. Security sign-off: PASS.

comments.note: MEDIUM | A02 — Cryptographic Failures | File: src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/Auth/Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs, lines 1-43. SHA-256 with a fixed compile-time application salt ('spdb_42') is not a password KDF. SHA-256 can be computed at billions of hashes/second on commodity hardware; the fixed salt is extractable from the compiled binary, enabling offline attacks with precomputed tables once the database file is obtained. Developer docstring explicitly acknowledges this trade-off ('local, single-user desktop application with no network-exposed authentication surface — practical risk is low'). The IPasswordHasher interface provides a clean upgrade path to Argon2id/bcrypt/PBKDF2 without caller changes. Recommendation: when attack-surface tolerance permits, replace with PBKDF2 (System.Security.Cryptography.Rfc2898DeriveBytes, SHA-256, 600_000 iterations + per-hash random salt) or Argon2id via a NuGet package. Does not block approval for current threat model.

LOW | A04 — Insecure Design | File: src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/Auth/Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs, line 40 (Verify method). IPasswordHasher.Verify uses string.Equals(OrdinalIgnoreCase) — a non-constant-time comparison. PasswordService.VerifyAsync correctly bypasses this method and uses CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals directly. However, the timing-vulnerable Verify method remains on the public API surface. Future callers invoking IPasswordHasher.Verify directly would unknowingly introduce a timing side-channel. Recommendation: mark Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.Verify as using a non-CT comparison in its docstring, or replace string.Equals with a FixedTimeEquals call on the encoded bytes.

INFO | A09 — Security Logging | File: src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/Auth/PasswordService.cs. No audit trail for password set or verification events. Adding ILogger calls (at Debug/Information level) for SetAsync and a Warning-level log for VerifyAsync failure would aid incident diagnosis without leaking sensitive data. Does not block approval.

comments.note: Fix-Forward: Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.Verify used non-constant-time string.Equals and had no docstring warning. Added a <remarks> block explicitly noting (1) the method is not constant-time, (2) callers with timing side-channel requirements should use Hash() + CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals directly, and (3) PasswordService already does this — do not call Verify from security-sensitive paths. This prevents future callers from accidentally introducing a timing side-channel by calling IPasswordHasher.Verify directly.

[documentation-forward] IPasswordHasher interface should document whether implementors are required to make Verify constant-time. Currently the contract is silent on this; the Security Auditor noted the default implementation is NOT constant-time. Adding a <remarks> note to the interface's Verify method that 'Implementations are not required to use constant-time comparison — callers with timing side-channel requirements must hash the candidate themselves and compare via CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals' would prevent misuse by future consumers of the abstraction.

PasswordService.VerifyAsync correctly encodes both hashes as UTF-8 bytes before passing to FixedTimeEquals. Both outputs of Hash() are always 64-char lowercase hex strings (256-bit SHA-256), so the byte arrays are always equal length. The length-equality precondition for FixedTimeEquals to guarantee constant-time is met by the hasher contract.
